quiz.q: After 2 L of irrigation for an alkali burn, you stop and immediately test the pH, which reads 7.2. What is the problem?
choices: The reading is too low and irrigation should continue
The pH strip cannot be used after anesthetic drops
Testing immediately measures the irrigation fluid rather than the eye; wait 5-10 minutes and recheck
A pH of 7.2 means alkali remains and surgery is needed
quiz.why: Residual irrigant on the surface gives a falsely normal reading, which is why the eye is allowed to equilibrate for 5 to 10 minutes before rechecking. The target range is 7.0 to 7.4, and anesthetic drops do not interfere with the strip.

quiz.q: A 38-year-old was grinding metal without eye protection and now has a red, painful eye with a small dark spot on the iris. Which order should you decline?
choices: Obtain a visual acuity
Perform tonometry to measure intraocular pressure
Place a rigid eye shield
Keep him nothing by mouth
quiz.why: Grinding metal is the classic history for a penetrating intraocular foreign body, and any pressure on a possibly open globe can extrude intraocular contents. Acuity, shielding and NPO status are all appropriate for a patient who may go to the operating room.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old reports that the vision in his left eye went black painlessly about 90 minutes ago, like a curtain falling. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Routine ophthalmology referral in the morning
Reassurance, since painless vision loss is usually benign
Treat it as a detached retina and place an eye shield
Treat it as a stroke of the eye: check glucose, obtain an ECG, activate the stroke pathway per protocol, and get ophthalmology now
quiz.why: Sudden painless monocular vision loss is central retinal artery occlusion until proven otherwise, and the retina tolerates only about 90 to 240 minutes of ischemia. It shares its causes with cerebral stroke, which is why these patients are worked up as stroke patients.

quiz.q: A patient with a corneal abrasion asks whether he can take home the numbing drops that made his eye feel so much better. What do you tell him?
choices: Yes, with instructions to use them sparingly
Yes, but only for 24 hours
No: topical anesthetics prevent corneal healing and repeated use causes ulceration, so they are for examination only
No, because they are only available by prescription from ophthalmology
quiz.why: Topical anesthetics are toxic to the corneal epithelium and abolish the pain that would otherwise warn the patient, so repeated home use leads to non-healing ulcers. The restriction is clinical, not administrative, and no short-duration exception makes it safe.

quiz.q: A 74-year-old on warfarin has been bleeding from the nose for 40 minutes. Which sequence is correct?
choices: Tip the head back, ice the bridge, pinch the bony part for 5 minutes
Sit him forward, have him blow out the clots, spray oxymetazoline, then pinch the soft part of the nose continuously for 10-15 minutes
Pack both nostrils immediately without attempting pressure
Hold pressure for 2 minutes, release to check, and repeat
quiz.why: Clots hold the vessel open, the vasoconstrictor shrinks it, and pressure must be on the compressible cartilage and uninterrupted. Tipping back fills the stomach and causes vomiting, packing skips the step that works most of the time, and checking every 2 minutes restarts the bleed.

quiz.q: A patient's nosebleed is coming from both nostrils, running steadily down the back of his throat, and has not slowed after 15 minutes of correct anterior pressure. What does this suggest?
choices: A posterior bleed, which needs posterior packing and admission for monitoring
That the pressure technique was wrong and should be repeated
A clotting disorder requiring immediate platelet transfusion
Nasal fracture
quiz.why: Bilateral brisk bleeding running down the pharynx that resists correct anterior pressure is the description of a posterior source, which packs differently and carries enough risk of hypoxia and airway compromise that these patients are admitted and monitored.

quiz.q: A 22-year-old has severe one-sided sore throat, cannot open his mouth fully, has a muffled voice, and the uvula is pushed to the opposite side. What are you setting up?
choices: A lumbar puncture tray
A nebulizer and peak flow meter
A cervical collar and backboard
Good light, topical anesthetic spray, an 18 gauge needle with a guard, a 10 mL syringe, a specimen container, and working suction the patient can hold
quiz.why: Trismus, a muffled voice and uvular deviation describe a peritonsillar abscess, which is aspirated or drained at the bedside. Suction matters most because pus is about to enter the mouth of a patient who already cannot swallow.

quiz.q: A 42-year-old has had a sore throat for 8 hours and now has fever, drooling, a muffled voice and soft stridor. He sits leaning forward and refuses to lie back. What is the correct management in the first minute?
choices: Lay him flat for a proper throat examination
Start an IV and draw blood cultures before anything else
Keep him upright and calm, stay at the bedside, and get anesthesia, ENT, the difficult airway cart and a surgical airway kit into the room
Give oral analgesia and reassess in 30 minutes
quiz.why: This is adult epiglottitis, where the airway can close suddenly and where distress, lying flat or pharyngeal instrumentation can precipitate obstruction. Nothing matters more than having the people and equipment for a difficult airway physically present.

quiz.q: Why is a patient with epistaxis asked to blow out clots before pressure is applied?
choices: To make the examination less painful
Because a clot holds the bleeding vessel open and prevents the vessel walls from apposing under pressure
To collect a specimen for culture
To confirm the bleeding is anterior rather than posterior
quiz.why: Clearing clot allows the vasoconstrictor to reach the mucosa and lets direct pressure actually compress the vessel. It feels counterintuitive to make a nose bleed more before making it stop, which is why the step is so often skipped.

quiz.q: A 61-year-old taking lisinopril for four years has tongue and lip swelling with no hives and no itching. Epinephrine, diphenhydramine and methylprednisolone have been given with no change after 20 minutes. What is the explanation?
choices: The epinephrine dose was too low and should be repeated intravenously
This is a delayed allergic reaction that needs more time
The diagnosis must be wrong, since angioedema always responds to epinephrine
This is bradykinin-mediated ACE inhibitor angioedema, which does not respond reliably to those drugs, so the priority is airway readiness
quiz.why: Bradykinin-mediated swelling has a different mechanism from histamine-mediated swelling, so the allergy drugs do not work and waiting for them to work wastes the time before the airway closes. Duration of therapy does not exclude the drug as the cause.

quiz.q: Which sequence of findings indicates a closing airway?
choices: Voice change, then difficulty swallowing secretions, then drooling, then stridor
Itching, then hives, then flushing, then wheeze
Cough, then fever, then sputum, then crackles
Hoarseness, then rhinorrhea, then sneezing, then congestion
quiz.why: Each step in that progression represents a smaller lumen, ending with the turbulent airflow that makes stridor. The other sequences describe allergic skin reactions, pneumonia and an upper respiratory infection, none of which track airway diameter.

quiz.q: A 9-year-old knocked out a permanent upper front tooth 20 minutes ago. His mother has it wrapped in a dry paper towel. What do you do?
choices: Scrub the root with gauze and place it in tap water
Discard it and arrange a dental implant referral
Handle it by the crown only, rinse gently with saline or milk if dirty, and place it in milk or Hank's solution while the provider prepares to reimplant
Place it in ice water to preserve it
quiz.why: The periodontal ligament cells on the root are what allow reattachment, and scrubbing, drying, plain water and ice all kill them. Reimplantation within 30 to 60 minutes offers the best chance, so speed and the right medium are everything.

quiz.q: A patient treated for anaphylaxis with one dose of intramuscular epinephrine is symptom-free at 2 hours and asks to leave. What is appropriate?
choices: Discharge now with an antihistamine prescription
Observe at least 4-6 hours for a biphasic reaction, then discharge with two autoinjectors, a hands-on demonstration and an allergist referral
Admit every anaphylaxis patient overnight
Discharge once the hives resolve, whatever the elapsed time
quiz.why: Biphasic reactions typically recur within 4 to 12 hours after full resolution, which is the reason for an observation period. Routine admission is not required for an uncomplicated reaction, and resolution of the rash says nothing about the risk of recurrence.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old with a dental infection has fever, a hard woody swelling under both sides of his jaw, an elevated tongue and cannot swallow his saliva. What is the concern?
choices: Ludwig's angina, a floor-of-mouth infection that threatens the airway
Mumps
A simple dental abscess for outpatient dental follow-up
Temporomandibular joint dysfunction
quiz.why: Bilateral submandibular induration with tongue elevation and an inability to handle secretions is Ludwig's angina, which closes airways from below the tongue. Mumps causes parotid swelling without airway threat, and no outpatient pathway is safe for a patient drooling from infection.

quiz.q: A 14-year-old has had sudden severe left testicular pain for 4 hours with vomiting. The testicle is high-riding and transverse. The ultrasound technologist is 45 minutes away. What is correct?
choices: Wait for the ultrasound before contacting urology
Send him back to the waiting room with analgesia
Notify urology now and pursue the ultrasound in parallel, because imaging must not delay operative exploration
Apply ice and reassess in an hour
quiz.why: The findings are classic torsion and the salvage rate falls steeply past 6 hours from onset, so the surgeon is notified on clinical suspicion rather than on imaging confirmation. Waiting, sending him out front, or icing all spend the window that decides whether the testicle survives.

quiz.q: A 63-year-old man cannot urinate and has suprapubic fullness. What is the first step?
choices: Place a 16 French Foley immediately
Order a CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Give IV fluids to stimulate urine production
Perform a bladder scan, since over 300-400 mL with an inability to void supports retention and a normal volume avoids an unnecessary catheter
quiz.why: The scan takes a minute, answers the question, and prevents catheters in patients who are not actually retaining. Fluids in a patient who cannot empty makes matters worse, and imaging does not answer the immediate question.

quiz.q: A 59-year-old with a known ureteral stone returns with a temperature of 39.0 C, heart rate 122 and systolic 96. Why is this different from her previous visits?
choices: The fever means the stone has passed
An infected obstructed kidney is sepsis in a closed space and requires urgent decompression, not antibiotics alone
It indicates a simple urinary tract infection treatable orally at home
It means imaging is no longer necessary
quiz.why: Pus trapped behind an obstruction cannot be reached by antibiotics or drained by the body, and these patients deteriorate quickly into septic shock. Imaging matters more than before because it locates the obstruction that must be relieved.

quiz.q: A man with sickle cell disease has had a painful rigid erection for 6 hours. Which supportive measure is wrong?
choices: Applying ice packs to the area
Keeping him warm
Giving IV fluids and analgesia
Calling urology urgently
quiz.why: Cold promotes sickling and worsens the vaso-occlusion causing the priapism, so ice is specifically avoided in these patients. Warmth, hydration, analgesia and urgent urology are all correct, with intervention wanted inside about 4 hours.

quiz.q: A diabetic man has severe perineal pain, dusky discolored scrotal skin, a crackling sensation under the skin, and a temperature of 39.4 C with a systolic of 88. What is this?
choices: A simple scrotal abscess for bedside drainage
Epididymitis requiring oral antibiotics
Testicular torsion
Fournier gangrene, a necrotizing infection requiring immediate surgery and resuscitation
quiz.why: Crepitus, dusky skin, disproportionate pain and shock describe a necrotizing soft tissue infection of the perineum, which is measured in hours and needs the operating room. Bedside drainage and oral antibiotics both lose time the patient does not have.

quiz.q: A 20-year-old football player collapses at practice. Rectal temperature is 41.3 C and he is confused and combative. What is the priority?
choices: Acetaminophen and IV fluids
Immediate aggressive cooling, targeting a core temperature under 39 C within 30 minutes
CT head before cooling, because of the altered mental status
A single ice pack to the groin and reassessment in 20 minutes
quiz.why: Outcome in heat stroke tracks total time above 40 C, so cooling begins before labs and imaging. Antipyretics do nothing because the hypothalamic set point is normal, and a single ice pack cannot move a core temperature quickly enough.

quiz.q: During cooling for heat stroke, the core temperature reaches 38.7 C. What should happen?
choices: Continue cooling until the temperature reaches 36.5 C
Switch from immersion to ice packs and keep going to 37 C
Stop active cooling, because continuing past about 38.5-39 C overshoots into hypothermia
Give acetaminophen to complete the normalization
quiz.why: Core temperature continues to fall after cooling stops, so pushing to normal produces iatrogenic hypothermia and its own arrhythmia risk. The endpoint is deliberately set slightly above normal, and antipyretics play no role at any stage.

quiz.q: A hypothermic patient at 26 C is being transferred from a stretcher to a bed. Why does technique matter so much?
choices: Rough handling can precipitate ventricular fibrillation in a cold, electrically irritable heart
Movement causes rapid rewarming and overshoot
The patient will feel severe pain despite being unconscious
It risks dislodging the esophageal temperature probe
quiz.why: Myocardial irritability in severe hypothermia is well described, and jostling has triggered fatal arrhythmias, which is why these patients are moved slowly and deliberately. Movement does not rewarm anyone, and probe position is trivial by comparison.

quiz.q: A hypothermic hiker is being rewarmed. Which approach avoids afterdrop?
choices: Immerse the hands and feet in warm water first
Apply heating pads to the arms and legs
Have the patient walk to increase muscle heat production
Apply forced-air warming and heating pads to the trunk rather than the extremities
quiz.why: Warming the limbs first dilates peripheral vessels and returns cold acidotic blood to the core, dropping the core temperature further. Truncal rewarming avoids that, and exertion in a severely hypothermic patient is both impossible and dangerous.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old was bitten on the forearm by a copperhead 30 minutes ago. Which combination is correct?
choices: Apply a proximal tourniquet and ice the bite site
Incise the fang marks and apply suction, then elevate the arm above the head
Remove all rings, mark the leading edge of swelling with the time and repeat every 15-30 minutes, immobilize the limb near heart level, and call Poison Control
Apply ice and give antivenom dosed by body weight
quiz.why: Marked, timed swelling progression tells the team whether the envenomation is advancing and whether antivenom is working, and rings must come off before swelling traps them. Tourniquets, ice and incision add tissue injury without removing venom, and antivenom is dosed by symptoms rather than weight.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old who is 7 weeks pregnant has cramping and light vaginal bleeding. Her blood type returns as A negative. What must not be missed?
choices: Rh immune globulin within 72 hours, which protects future pregnancies
A tetanus booster
Immediate transfusion of O negative blood
Methotrexate before discharge
quiz.why: Bleeding in pregnancy can sensitize an Rh-negative patient to Rh-positive fetal cells, endangering later pregnancies, and prevention only works inside 72 hours. Transfusion depends on her hemoglobin and stability, and methotrexate treats a confirmed ectopic pregnancy.

quiz.q: A 31-year-old woman who delivered three weeks ago returns with a severe headache, blurred vision and a blood pressure of 176/112. What is the leading concern?
choices: Migraine with aura
Postpartum preeclampsia, which can occur up to 6 weeks after delivery
Tension headache from sleep deprivation
Benign postpartum hypertension requiring no treatment
quiz.why: Preeclampsia does not end at delivery and the postpartum version is the one emergency departments miss, because the patient no longer looks pregnant. Headache and visual change with a pressure this high are severe features and need magnesium and blood pressure control.

quiz.q: A patient at 34 weeks is receiving a magnesium infusion for severe preeclampsia. Which finding appears first if she becomes toxic?
choices: Respiratory depression
Cardiac arrest
Falling urine output
Loss of deep tendon reflexes
quiz.why: Reflexes disappear before respiratory depression, which precedes cardiac effects, which is why reflexes are checked repeatedly during an infusion. Calcium gluconate is the antidote and should already be in the room before the magnesium starts.

quiz.q: During an unplanned delivery the head delivers but the anterior shoulder does not follow. What is correct?
choices: Apply firm fundal pressure
Apply steady downward traction on the head until the shoulder releases
Flex the mother's knees sharply toward her chest and apply suprapubic pressure
Sit her fully upright and have her push harder
quiz.why: The McRoberts maneuver rotates the pelvis and, with suprapubic pressure, frees the anterior shoulder from behind the pubic bone. Fundal pressure drives the shoulder harder against the bone, and traction on the head risks a brachial plexus injury.

quiz.q: A patient at 36 weeks arrives with a loop of umbilical cord visible at the introitus. What do you do?
choices: Attempt to replace the cord back into the vagina
Place her in knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg, and hold the presenting part off the cord with a gloved hand until the surgical team takes over
Clamp and cut the cord to prevent further prolapse
Have her sit upright and push
quiz.why: Cord prolapse compresses fetal circulation, so the only useful maneuver is physically lifting the presenting part off the cord and keeping it there through transfer to an immediate cesarean. Replacing, clamping or encouraging descent all worsen the compression.

quiz.q: An 86-year-old on rivaroxaban tripped on a curb, struck her forehead, and has a completely normal neurological examination. What should you expect?
choices: Discharge with head injury instructions
Skull X-rays
Observation for 1 hour then discharge
CT of the head, because anticoagulation allows significant intracranial bleeding after a trivial mechanism with a normal exam
quiz.why: Anticoagulated patients bleed from minor forces and can appear entirely normal while a hematoma expands, so imaging is driven by the drug rather than the examination. Skull films do not exclude intracranial bleeding and brief observation without imaging misses delayed bleeds.

quiz.q: An 88-year-old man on metoprolol arrives after a fall with a heart rate of 74 and a blood pressure of 126/72. His daughter says his pressure normally runs 175. How should you read this?
choices: As a significant drop from his own baseline, with the beta blocker masking the tachycardia that would normally signal bleeding
As reassuring, since both values are within population normal limits
As evidence of dehydration only
As evidence that his beta blocker dose is too high
quiz.why: Normal limits are population values, and a chronic hypertensive perfusing at 175 may be shocked at 126. Beta blockade removes the compensatory tachycardia, so both numbers that would normally raise alarm are silenced in this patient.

quiz.q: A 29-year-old brought in after a bar fight smells of alcohol, has a GCS of 13, and a scalp laceration. A colleague suggests letting him sleep it off. What is correct?
choices: Let him sleep and reassess in 4 hours
Send a blood alcohol level and discharge when it falls below the legal limit
Treat him as head-injured until imaging proves otherwise, check a glucose, undress and examine him fully, and document serial examinations
Apply restraints and recheck at shift change
quiz.why: Attributing altered mental status to alcohol before imaging is how intracranial bleeds are missed, and intoxication also masks pain from other injuries. Sobriety is judged by serial examination rather than by a number or a clock, and restraint is not assessment.

quiz.q: An 81-year-old was found on her bathroom floor and does not know how long she was there. Which complication should you specifically ask about and look for?
choices: Delayed splenic rupture
Rhabdomyolysis, pressure injury, hypothermia and dehydration from a prolonged lie
Fat embolism syndrome
Compartment syndrome of the abdomen
quiz.why: A long lie causes muscle breakdown that injures the kidneys, skin damage over bony points, heat loss to the floor, and fluid depletion, all of which are missed if nobody asks how long the patient was down. The other entities have different mechanisms and are not typical of a ground-level fall.

quiz.q: Why can an intoxicated trauma patient not be clinically cleared of a cervical spine injury?
choices: Intoxicated patients always have neck injuries
Alcohol causes false positive imaging
Cervical collars cannot be applied to uncooperative patients
The clinical decision rules require a reliable, sober patient who can accurately report pain and distracting injury
quiz.why: Rules like NEXUS and the Canadian C-spine rule depend on a patient who can report midline tenderness and has no distracting injury, and intoxication invalidates both conditions. Imaging or serial reassessment after sobriety is therefore required.

quiz.q: A 20-month-old with a barky cough has stridor only when crying and none at rest. What is the most useful approach?
choices: Keep him calm on a parent's lap, give dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, and watch specifically for stridor at rest
Lay him flat and examine the pharynx with a tongue depressor
Start high-flow nasal cannula immediately
Obtain a chest X-ray and a viral panel
quiz.why: Stridor only with agitation is milder croup, and a single dose of dexamethasone plus a calm child is the standard approach with stridor at rest as the escalation marker. Instrumenting the pharynx risks obstruction, and imaging and viral testing rarely change management.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old asthmatic has been wheezing loudly for 45 minutes. His chest is now quiet and he has become drowsy. What does this represent?
choices: Successful bronchodilation and a reason to step down care
Normal fatigue after the work of breathing
Too little airflow to generate a wheeze, with drowsiness from carbon dioxide retention: impending respiratory failure
Incorrect stethoscope placement
quiz.why: Wheeze requires turbulent airflow, so its disappearance alongside clinical deterioration means airflow has collapsed. Sleepiness in an asthmatic child is carbon dioxide narcosis, not rest, and the pair together is a resuscitation.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old with croup improves dramatically 20 minutes after racemic epinephrine, and the family wants to leave. What is correct?
choices: Discharge now, since the treatment worked
Observe for 2-3 hours, because the drug wears off before the airway swelling does and symptoms can rebound
Give a second dose and discharge
Admit every child who receives racemic epinephrine
quiz.why: Racemic epinephrine constricts mucosal vessels temporarily without treating the underlying inflammation, so rebound stridor can occur as it wears off. A defined observation period detects that, while routine admission is not required for a child who remains well.

quiz.q: A previously well 2-year-old suddenly coughed violently while eating peanuts and now has decreased breath sounds on the right with a unilateral wheeze. What is the concern?
choices: Bronchiolitis
Pneumonia
Croup
An aspirated foreign body, which needs rigid bronchoscopy
quiz.why: A sudden choking event during eating followed by unilateral findings is the classic foreign body story, and bronchoscopy is both the diagnosis and the treatment. Bronchiolitis and pneumonia develop over days with bilateral or focal infectious findings, and croup causes inspiratory stridor rather than a one-sided wheeze.

quiz.q: A 3-month-old with bronchiolitis has copious nasal secretions, a respiratory rate of 62 and mild retractions. Which simple intervention is likely to help most?
choices: Nasal suction, because infants are obligate nose breathers and a blocked nose is a genuine cause of distress
A loading dose of oral steroids
An immediate chest X-ray
Restraining the infant flat to obtain accurate vital signs
quiz.why: Clearing the nose improves work of breathing and feeding in a large fraction of infants with bronchiolitis. Steroids do not benefit typical bronchiolitis, routine imaging rarely changes management, and flat restraint worsens both distress and the accuracy of the numbers.

quiz.q: A dialysis patient who missed two sessions has a potassium of 7.4 with peaked T waves and a widening QRS. Which drug goes first, and why?
choices: Insulin with dextrose, because it lowers the potassium level
Nebulized albuterol, because it acts fastest
Calcium gluconate, because it stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes even though it does not lower potassium
Sodium bicarbonate, because it corrects the acidosis
quiz.why: With ECG changes the immediate threat is a fatal arrhythmia, and calcium protects the myocardium within minutes while insulin and albuterol take 15 to 30 minutes to shift potassium. Bicarbonate has a narrower role and no immediate membrane effect.

quiz.q: A potassium of 6.3 returns on a well-appearing outpatient, and the laboratory has flagged the specimen as hemolyzed. What is correct?
choices: Treat for hyperkalemia immediately
Redraw the specimen with good technique and obtain an ECG while waiting for the result
Ignore the result and discharge the patient
Rerun the same specimen on a different analyzer
quiz.why: Hemolysis releases potassium from red cells and falsely elevates the result, so treating it risks causing hypokalemia. Ignoring it risks missing real hyperkalemia, which is why the ECG is obtained while the redraw processes. Rerunning a damaged sample changes nothing.

quiz.q: A hemodialysis patient with a left forearm arteriovenous fistula needs an IV and blood work. What is correct?
choices: Use the fistula, since it is already a large vessel
Use the fistula arm for the blood pressure but a different site for the IV
Use the fistula only for the blood draw and not for infusion
Use the opposite arm for the IV, the blood draw and the blood pressure, and never the fistula arm
quiz.why: Any cannulation, compression or blood pressure on a fistula arm risks thrombosing an access the patient depends on to stay alive. The restriction applies to every use of that arm, not just to infusions.

quiz.q: A patient received insulin and dextrose for hyperkalemia 45 minutes ago. What must be checked?
choices: Glucose at 30 and 60 minutes, because hypoglycemia occurs when the dextrose clears before the insulin does
A repeat chest X-ray
Deep tendon reflexes
A repeat blood type and screen
quiz.why: Insulin outlasts the dextrose given with it, so delayed hypoglycemia is the predictable complication and the one most often caught by the person taking the glucose readings. Reflexes are monitored during magnesium infusions, not insulin.

quiz.q: An 81-year-old admitted for pneumonia has been boarding in an ED bed for 16 hours. Which set of tasks is yours?
choices: None; the admitting team now owns her care entirely
Turning every 2 hours with heels floated, confirming home medications have been addressed, orientation with glasses and hearing aids in, toileting, and vitals on the admitted schedule
Only repeat vital signs at the original ED interval
Removing the IV and telemetry since she is leaving soon
quiz.why: Until the patient physically leaves, the department is responsible, and the specific harms of boarding are pressure injuries, missed medications and delirium, all prevented by exactly this work. Removing lines and monitoring from an admitted patient is not a technician decision.

scenarios.title: At the desk: concrete in both eyes
scenarios.intro: A `34`-year-old mason is walked in by a coworker with his face soaked and both eyes clamped shut. He says wet concrete went into both eyes about `6` minutes ago when a mixer kicked. He is in severe pain and cannot open either lid. Registration is asking for his insurance card.

steps.prompt:
He is standing at the desk, bent over, hands over his face. The nurse is with another patient.

What do you do?

choices.text: Bring him to a room, get a visual acuity in each eye, then start irrigation
choices.feedback: Acuity is normally the vital sign of the eye, and this is the one situation where it waits. Wet concrete is an alkali and it is still dissolving his corneas while you hold up a chart.

choices.text: Get him to the nearest sink or eyewash and start irrigating now, and ask someone to bring anesthetic drops and a Morgan lens setup to you
choices.feedback: Correct. Irrigation outranks everything, including acuity and registration. Starting at a sink while the proper setup is brought to you loses no time at all.

choices.text: Let registration finish so he has an armband before treatment starts
choices.feedback: This is a treat-before-you-register emergency. Every minute of paperwork is a minute the alkali keeps tunneling deeper.

choices.text: Take him straight back, call for the nurse and the Morgan lens setup, and start irrigating with saline while you wait
choices.feedback: Also right. The key move is that fluid is running within seconds and the formal setup catches up.

steps.prompt:
Saline is running. He is fighting you because it hurts and he cannot keep the lids open. The nurse arrives with tetracaine and a Morgan lens.

What comes next?

choices.text: Instill topical anesthetic first, then place the Morgan lens with the flow already running, seating it under the upper lid first
choices.feedback: Exactly. Nobody can hold a chemically burned eye open without anesthetic, and starting the flow before the lens goes in stops it scraping a raw cornea.

choices.text: Place the Morgan lens dry, then start the flow once it is seated
choices.feedback: A dry lens dragged across a burned cornea is its own injury. Flow starts before the lens goes in and stops before it comes out.

choices.text: Hold the lids open by force and keep pouring saline from a bottle
choices.feedback: Pouring from a bottle delivers almost nothing and forcing the lids on an unanesthetized burn will not be tolerated for the litres this needs.

choices.text: Anesthetize, then check a pH strip in the lower lid pocket before continuing so there is a baseline
choices.feedback: Reasonable and commonly done, as long as it takes seconds and the flow restarts immediately. A baseline pH does help show progress.

steps.prompt:
Both eyes have now had `2 L` of saline. He is calmer and can open his eyes a little. You notice gritty white particles in the folds under both upper lids.

What do you do?

choices.text: Stop irrigation and check the pH, since 2 L is the standard volume
choices.feedback: Volume is not the endpoint here. Retained cement particles are a reservoir of alkali that will keep burning after you stop, and they have to come out.

choices.text: Evert the upper lids and sweep the fornices to remove the particles, then continue irrigating
choices.feedback: Right. Lime and cement leave grit in the lid pockets that keeps the pH up no matter how much fluid you run. Sweeping is part of the treatment.

choices.text: Apply antibiotic ointment to trap the particles and refer to ophthalmology
choices.feedback: Ointment seals alkali against the cornea. Nothing goes on until the particles are out and the pH has normalized.

choices.text: Tell the provider about the particles and ask for help with lid eversion while irrigation continues
choices.feedback: Good. Lid eversion with a cooperative anesthetized patient is straightforward, and asking for a second pair of hands keeps the fluid running throughout.

steps.prompt:
The fornices are clear and you have run a further `1 L` in each eye. You stop the flow and immediately test the pH, which reads `7.2` in both eyes.

What do you conclude?

choices.text: The burn is neutralized; remove the lenses and get an acuity
choices.feedback: A pH checked the instant you stop measures the irrigation fluid sitting on the surface, not the eye. This number is not trustworthy yet.

choices.text: Wait 5-10 minutes with the flow off, then recheck the pH, aiming for a stable 7.0-7.4
choices.feedback: Correct. The surface has to equilibrate before the strip tells you anything about the eye. Rechecking at 5-10 minutes is the step that catches an ongoing burn.

choices.text: Continue irrigating for another 2 L regardless, since alkali burns always need more
choices.feedback: More fluid is sometimes right, but the decision is made on a valid pH, not on a rule of thumb. Wait and recheck first.

choices.text: Add a buffering solution to neutralize the remaining alkali
choices.feedback: Chemical neutralization generates heat and further injury. Dilution with a neutral fluid is the only correct approach.

steps.prompt:
Ten minutes later the pH is `7.1` in both eyes and stable. The lenses come out. Now you can get a visual acuity: `20/70` on the right, `20/40` on the left with his own glasses.

What goes in the chart and what happens next?

choices.text: Just the final acuity and that irrigation was performed
choices.feedback: Too thin. Nobody reading this later can tell how long the alkali was in contact, how much fluid was used, or whether the pH was ever verified.

choices.text: Time of exposure, the substance, time irrigation started, total volume per eye, that the fornices were swept, each pH with its time, and the acuity with the time it was taken
choices.feedback: Complete. Every one of those items changes how ophthalmology manages him, and the contact time in particular predicts the injury.

choices.text: The acuity, plus a note that he was discharged once comfortable
choices.feedback: He is not going home on your say-so. An alkali burn with reduced acuity in both eyes needs ophthalmology, and the disposition is not a technician's call.

choices.text: The full irrigation record, and tell the provider his acuity is reduced in both eyes so ophthalmology can be called
choices.feedback: Right. Reduced acuity after an alkali exposure is the finding that gets ophthalmology to the bedside, and it needs saying out loud rather than only charting.

scenarios.debrief:
Chemical eye exposure is one of a very small number of complaints where treatment begins before identification, before acuity and before a room. The rule is simple and it is constantly broken by people trying to be orderly: fluid runs first.

Three details separate a good irrigation from a ritual one. The anesthetic, because nobody tolerates litres of fluid on a burned cornea without it. The lid sweep, because cement, lime and plaster leave particles in the fornices that keep releasing alkali no matter how much saline you run. And the delayed pH recheck, because a strip read the second you stop the flow is measuring your saline, not his eye.

Alkali is the reason all of this is urgent. Acid burns the surface and partly seals itself; alkali dissolves cell membranes and keeps going deeper for exactly as long as it is present.

scenarios.title: Triage: 15-year-old with 'stomach pain' he will not discuss
scenarios.intro: A `15`-year-old boy is brought in by his mother for abdominal pain and vomiting that started about `3` hours ago while he was playing video games. He is pale, will not sit still, and answers in one word. His mother does most of the talking. Triage has him as an abdominal pain, waiting-room appropriate.

steps.prompt:
He is doubled over in the triage chair. His mother says he has been vomiting and that it came on suddenly.

What do you do?

choices.text: Ask him directly, and privately, whether the pain is anywhere else, specifically in the groin or testicle
choices.feedback: This is the question that changes the case. Teenage boys routinely present torsion as abdominal pain and will not volunteer the location, especially with a parent in the room.

choices.text: Chart the vitals and leave him in the waiting room with the other abdominal pains
choices.feedback: Sudden severe pain with vomiting in a 15-year-old is not a waiting-room complaint, and you have not yet asked the one question that would reclassify him.

choices.text: Ask his mother whether he has been constipated
choices.feedback: You are asking the wrong person and pursuing the wrong diagnosis. The history you need is his, and it is private.

choices.text: Move him to a room first so there is privacy, then take a proper history from him alone
choices.feedback: Good instinct. Getting him out of the waiting room costs nothing and gives you the privacy that makes the real history possible.

steps.prompt:
With his mother briefly out of the room he tells you the pain is really in his left testicle, that it woke him from a nap, and that this has happened twice before but went away on its own within an hour.

What do you do with that?

choices.text: Reassure him that it resolved before and will probably resolve again
choices.feedback: Previous episodes that resolved are intermittent torsion, which is a risk factor, not reassurance. This time it has not resolved in three hours.

choices.text: Tell the charge nurse and the provider out loud, using the words 'possible testicular torsion', and get him into a treatment bed now
choices.feedback: Correct. Saying the words is what changes the trajectory of the case. Torsion has roughly a six-hour window and he is already three hours in.

choices.text: Order an ultrasound yourself and wait for the result before telling anyone
choices.feedback: Ordering is not your role, and more importantly imaging must never be the step that delays the surgical page. Escalate first.

choices.text: Report it immediately and ask whether they want urology paged while imaging is arranged
choices.feedback: Very good. Suggesting that the page and the scan run in parallel is exactly the thinking that saves the testicle.

steps.prompt:
The provider examines him: the left testicle is high, lying sideways, exquisitely tender, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. Elevation makes it worse. Doppler ultrasound is booked but the technologist is `35 minutes` out.

What is the right move?

choices.text: Wait for the ultrasound; urology will not accept a patient without imaging
choices.feedback: The exam here is classic and the clock is running. Surgeons take these calls on clinical suspicion, and waiting for a scan is how testicles are lost.

choices.text: Page urology now on the clinical findings, and let the ultrasound happen in parallel
choices.feedback: Right. Parallel, never sequential. Imaging can confirm while the operating room is being arranged, and if imaging is delayed further the exam alone is enough.

choices.text: Give him pain medication and reassess in an hour
choices.feedback: He needs analgesia, but not instead of the surgical page. An hour of observation is a sixth of the entire salvage window.

choices.text: Page urology, give analgesia and an antiemetic, and keep him nothing by mouth for the operating room
choices.feedback: Excellent. All three of those happen together: the page, the comfort measures, and the preparation for surgery you are already expecting.

steps.prompt:
Urology is coming. The mother asks you what is happening and why everyone suddenly moved so fast, and the patient is embarrassed and asking whether he has to have surgery.

How do you handle this?

choices.text: Tell them the testicle is probably dead and he will lose it
choices.feedback: That is not your prognosis to give, and it is not accurate at three to four hours. Do not hand a family a conclusion the surgeon has not reached.

choices.text: Explain in plain words that the blood supply may be twisted, that it is time-sensitive, that the surgeon is on the way, and that they will explain the plan
choices.feedback: Right level. Honest, plain, does not exceed your scope, and it explains the urgency the family just witnessed without frightening them with specifics you cannot promise.

choices.text: Say you cannot discuss anything and the doctor will explain later
choices.feedback: Technically safe, humanly poor. A family watching a room move at speed deserves an honest general explanation, and silence reads as something being hidden.

choices.text: Explain the urgency plainly, and separately tell the patient that this is a common problem in boys his age and he did the right thing by telling you
choices.feedback: Very good. The embarrassment is the reason these cases present late, and normalizing it makes the next teenager more likely to speak up.

steps.prompt:
He goes to the operating room `4 hours and 20 minutes` after the pain began. The testicle is detorsed and viable, and both sides are fixed in place.

Looking back, what was the single decision that mattered most?

choices.text: Getting the ultrasound booked quickly
choices.feedback: The ultrasound never changed the plan. It was arranged in parallel and could have been skipped entirely on the strength of the exam.

choices.text: Asking a teenage boy, privately and directly, where the pain actually was
choices.feedback: That is the case. Everything downstream followed from one private question asked in a triage chair, on a patient labelled as abdominal pain.

choices.text: Giving analgesia early so he could cooperate with the exam
choices.feedback: Humane and helpful, and not the decision that saved the testicle. He would have been examined either way.

choices.text: Refusing to let imaging delay the urology page
choices.feedback: This one genuinely mattered too. A 35-minute wait for a scan inside a six-hour window is exactly the kind of sequential thinking that costs organs.

scenarios.debrief:
Torsion is a clock that starts before the patient reaches the building, and this case was won in the first two minutes by a question rather than a test. Adolescent boys present torsion as abdominal pain constantly, they will not raise the real location in front of a parent, and the triage label they arrive with is frequently wrong.

The second lesson is about sequence. Imaging and the surgical page are run in parallel, never one after the other, because a classic examination is already enough to justify the call and a scanner that is 35 minutes away is a sixth of the salvage window. Previous episodes that resolved on their own are intermittent torsion, which raises the risk rather than lowering it.

The third is quieter. Embarrassment is why these patients present late, so how you ask and how you respond to the answer is part of the medicine.

scenarios.title: Room 11: 79-year-old found on the kitchen floor
scenarios.intro: EMS brings a `79`-year-old woman found by her daughter on the kitchen floor. She does not remember falling and does not know how long she was down. She is alert, oriented to person and place, and complains only of a sore shoulder. Her daughter says she takes "a few heart pills" and looks after herself.

steps.prompt:
Her vitals look unremarkable at first glance. The daughter is keen to take her home once the shoulder is checked.

Which question matters most right now?

choices.text: Which shoulder is sore
choices.feedback: You will need it, but it is not the question that changes the case. A shoulder is the complaint she can articulate, not the reason she is on the floor.

choices.text: Did she trip, or did she black out
choices.feedback: This is the fork in the road. A mechanical fall is a trauma case. A syncopal fall is a cardiac case with bruises, and the two get completely different workups.

choices.text: Whether she has had her flu shot
choices.feedback: Not now. There is a patient in front of you who does not remember falling, which is itself a finding.

choices.text: What medications she takes, by name, especially any blood thinner
choices.feedback: Also critical, and a close second. Anticoagulation changes the imaging threshold for every part of this case.

steps.prompt:
She says she does not remember anything between putting the kettle on and her daughter finding her. You ask about blood thinners and she says no. Her daughter pulls out a pill organizer containing metoprolol, atorvastatin and apixaban.

What do you do?

choices.text: Accept her answer, since patients know their own medications
choices.feedback: Patients routinely answer no to 'blood thinner' while taking one, because they think of the word as meaning warfarin or aspirin. Ask by drug name and check the bottles.

choices.text: Report immediately that she is on apixaban and that she has an unwitnessed head-down fall with amnesia
choices.feedback: Exactly right. A factor Xa inhibitor turns a minor mechanism into a CT, and the amnesia means nobody can exclude a head strike.

choices.text: Note the apixaban in the chart and mention it at handoff
choices.feedback: Charting it is necessary and insufficient. This is the single fact most likely to change the next hour of her care, so it gets said out loud now.

choices.text: Report the apixaban and ask the daughter to photograph every bottle at home so the list is complete
choices.feedback: Good thinking. A verified medication list matters here, and the beta blocker in that organizer is about to matter too.

steps.prompt:
The provider orders a CT head and cervical spine. While you undress her for a full examination, her daughter says her blood pressure is normally "about one seventy" and that the doctor has been trying to bring it down for years.

What does that do to your reading of a pressure of `132/78` with a heart rate of `72`?

choices.text: Nothing; both numbers are within normal limits
choices.feedback: Normal limits are population values. A chronic hypertensive who perfuses at 170 may be shocked at 132, and her metoprolol is preventing the tachycardia that would normally announce it.

choices.text: It is a substantial fall from her own baseline, and the beta blocker is masking the heart rate response, so this may be occult bleeding
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts. Both of the numbers that would normally raise alarm have been silenced, one by chronic hypertension and one by a drug.

choices.text: It means her antihypertensives are finally working
choices.feedback: A pressure that improves on the day someone is found unconscious on a floor is not a treatment success.

choices.text: It raises concern for hidden blood loss, so report it with her baseline attached and look carefully for injuries she has not mentioned
choices.feedback: Very good. Reporting a number with its baseline is what makes it meaningful, and the physical search is how you find what she cannot tell you.

steps.prompt:
Undressed, she has a large bruise over her right hip, a scalp laceration hidden in her hair that nobody had found, and the skin over her sacrum and both heels is red and non-blanching. She still says only her shoulder hurts.

What do you report and do?

choices.text: The shoulder pain and the hip bruise
choices.feedback: You found three things she never mentioned and you are reporting two. The scalp wound and the pressure changes both matter, and one of them tells you how long she was down.

choices.text: All of it: the hip bruise, the scalp laceration with active anticoagulation, and the non-blanching skin over the sacrum and heels indicating a prolonged lie
choices.feedback: Complete. The scalp wound proves a head strike in a patient on apixaban, and the pressure changes are objective evidence of hours on a hard floor.

choices.text: Cover her back up and let the provider find these on their own examination
choices.feedback: The primary reason to undress a patient is to find what they cannot report, and a finding you noticed and did not report is worse than one nobody looked for.

choices.text: Report the findings and add that a prolonged lie raises the question of rhabdomyolysis, dehydration and hypothermia
choices.feedback: Excellent. The long lie is its own diagnosis, and naming the consequences prompts the creatine kinase, the fluids and the temperature.

steps.prompt:
The CT shows a small acute subdural hematoma. She is going to be admitted. Her daughter, who has been at the bedside all along, mentions quietly that her mother has fallen "three or four times" this year and that she has started sleeping in the recliner because she cannot get upstairs.

What do you do with that?

choices.text: Nothing; falls are common at her age
choices.feedback: Four falls in a year is not ageing, it is a pattern with a cause: medications, arrhythmia, deconditioning, vision, or something at home. It is also a marker of risk for the next one.

choices.text: Report the fall history and the change in how she is living, because repeated falls point to a treatable cause and to an unsafe home situation
choices.feedback: Right. Recurrent falls plus a change in function is exactly the history that drives a syncope workup, a medication review and a safety assessment before discharge.

choices.text: Tell the daughter she should consider a nursing home
choices.feedback: Not your recommendation to make, and it shuts down a family member who was just starting to tell you useful things.

choices.text: Report it, and separately find a moment to speak with the patient alone as part of routine practice
choices.feedback: Good. Interviewing an older patient alone is standard, not an accusation, and it is the only way an abuse or neglect concern surfaces.

scenarios.debrief:
This patient arrived labelled as a sore shoulder and left with a subdural hematoma, a prolonged lie and an unexplained loss of consciousness. Nothing about her presentation was dramatic, which is the point.

Four ideas did all the work. First, trip or black out, because a syncopal fall is a cardiac case wearing trauma clothes. Second, ask about anticoagulation by drug name and look at the bottles, because half the patients taking one will say no. Third, read the vital signs against the patient's own baseline: a pressure of 132 in someone who lives at 170, with a beta blocker preventing the tachycardia, is two alarms that have both been switched off. Fourth, undress and look, because the findings that mattered most were a scalp wound hidden in hair and non-blanching skin over the sacrum, neither of which she mentioned or could see.

The last step is the one people skip. Recurrent falls with a change in function is a history that deserves a cause and a plan, not a discharge.
